newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU farm reforms rely on Fischler footwork.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU farm reforms rely on Fischler footwork.

text.p: Austrian Franz Fischler will need nimble political footwork, stamina and stubbornness to push plans for further cuts in farm prices past Europe's hostile agriculture ministers.

The burly, bearded European Union farm commissioner is determined to fight for the European Commission's "Agenda 2000" programme and reforms to prepare for the entry of former communist countries to the bloc.

"It will be a long, hard battle," he said after nearly all EU farm ministers last month attacked the Agenda 2000 proposals to cut dairy, cereals and beef prices by up to 30 percent with only partial compensation to farmers.
Fischler is likely to stand the strain.

After an overnight flight following a recent gruelling trip to the United States, he immediately faced the European Parliament for several hours of sometimes obscure questioning on farm policy and ploughed on with a hectic work schedule far into the evening.

Although Britain, one of the few supporters of reform, has pledged to give the proposals priority during its EU presidency in the first half of next year, a breakthrough is unlikely until after German elections in late 1998.
NO ROOM FOR COMPROMISE
Fischler, displaying the rugged resolve typical of Tyroleans, has ruled out the classic watered-down EU compromise, saying there was little room for manoeuvre.
"I can't accept suggestions that will dilute it so much that it no longer tastes like wine," he said. Agenda 2000 is a coherent package that cannot be picked apart, he added.
Fischler, 50, has tried to calm fears that EU farm spending could spiral out of control as low-cost east European farmers seize advantage of EU subsidies and send production surging.
He also argues that unless the EU prices to world levels it will be unable to export freely and share in an expected increase in world demand.
High-priced EU farm exports require subsidies in order to compete on world markets and such shipments are subject to limits enforced by the World Trade Organisation.
Since taking over the hot seat of EU agriculture in January 1995, Fischler has steered safely through several storms.

When the British government dropped a bombshell in March 1996 by admitting that so-called mad cow disease could spread to humans, causing a similar brain-wasting illness, Fischler moved fast to impose a worldwide ban on British beef exports.
In the following months he worked hard to protect public health and tried to satisfy Britain's demands for a gradual lifting of the ban while fending off attacks from the European Parliament.

Although coming from a new member state, Fischler was well equipped for his key post in agriculture -- which accounts for more than half the EU's annual budget -- with a doctorate in agriculture and five years as Austrian farm minister.
Fischler had already shown considerable skill in winning favourable terms for Austrian farmers when they joined an overwhelming two-thirds Austrian "yes" vote for membership in June 1994.
"Fischler managed to delve out concessions others thought were impossible," one Austrian official said.
Austrian farmers have since complained increasingly that Fischler has not championed their interests.

However, reflecting his roots in a country of mainly small-scale mountain farmers, Fischler has promoted integrated rural development in which farmers protect the countryside and cater for tourists as well as produce food.
Although the so-called Cork Declaration setting out his rural vision received a stony reception in capitals and from farmers, Fischler refused to drop his ideas and is working hard to resurrect them.
Sensitive to Austrian hostility to genetically engineered food, Fischler has also fought for strict rules on clear labelling and segregation of genetically modified organisms.

HOME PAGE ON But he is quick to use new technology and is one of the first EUU commissioners to have a home page on the Internet with a picture portrait and invitation to readers to send their views by e-mail.

During marathon farm ministers' meetings, he has been tough and persistent in hammering out agreements. At times he has also had to backtrack -- recently on cuts in aid to grain farmers when these proved politically unacceptable.
"His thick hide, which has made him immune to intrigues, will also prove very useful to him at a European level," commented one Viennese newspaper.
Fischler stays in close contact with Austrian politics, retaining an office in Vienna, and as a senior member of the conservative People's Party is tipped as a possible vice chancellor.
He continues to keep a close eye on his four hectare (9.8 acres) forestry estate, flying most weekends to his home in the Alpine village of Absam to join his wife and four children.

Although his EU mandate expires at the end of 1999, the bon vivant former farmer has shown a healthy appetite for the job and enjoys Brussels' gourmet restaurants. Sources say he could stay, though not necessarily in the same post.
